utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now bring in the witness, who will be testifying without protective measures. The Prosecution, as I have said, shouldn't take more than an hour and a half, which should be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that the equipment is functioning properly. If you're receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please speak up, because the interpreters did not hear you. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you very well. I have understood you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, you've been called here to testify on behalf of the Prosecution. Please stand up since you will now have to take the solemn declaration. Could you tell me your first and last names and your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My name is Hasan Hasic. I was born on the 1st of January, 1939.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm currently retired, but I'm still involved in agricultural labour. I also used to work as -- as a haulier, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, have you already testified in The Hague or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the first time. This is the first time ever that I have come to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you been interrogated by investigators in your own country or have you only been interviewed by OTP investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in my own country, but I suppose they were representatives of the Tribunal, and similarly they came to visit me in Germany when I was there in the 1990s -- or, rather, I was there from 1994 until the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you please read out the solemn declaration that the usher will show to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. There's nothing else I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll provide you with some information about the procedure that we will be following today. You will first of all have to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution. You must have met the Prosecution yesterday or this morning. The Prosecution has an hour and a half for their examination-in-chief and to show you documents. Then the Defence, who you are to your left, will also have about an hour and a half to put questions to you, and some of the accused might also put questions to you during the time allocated to them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've understood that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the four Judges who are sitting before you may also ask you to clarify certain issues or put questions to you, because they believe that your testimony or parts of your testimony are of great importance, and as a result the Judges will then put questions to you. If you run into difficulties of any kind, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact. We are here to ensure that you testify under the best possible conditions. Try to provide full and precise answers, because what --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, whatever I can tell you I'll it tell you. I'll put things as clearly as possible. I have understood everything you have said, and I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because what we want to find out from you is who did what and how things happened, and this is the information we would like to obtain through your testimony. As I have said, if you feel there are problems of any kind, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact. Having said that, I will now give the floor to the Prosecution so that they can start their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Sir --

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you were born and raised in the village of Recice, municipality of Capljina?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Recica, is that part of Domanovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: It's in Domanovici. My house is 300 or 400 metres from Domanovici, so one could say that it's all one place almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And Domanovici and Recice are both situated on the Dubrave plateau?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The Dubrave plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: In July, 1993, you were also -- or you will still residing in Recice?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Up until the 13th or 14th of July. That's when I left, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, dealing with a few biographical details, is it correct that you married in 1968 and you had five children?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have five children, two -- two boys, but one after three days and another after three months died but the three daughters are alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. So your two boys died in infancy, but in 1993 your three daughters were still alive.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. As babies, yes. Up until the 13th of July, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, on the 13th of July, could you tell us what the ages of your three daughters, Sanela, Dzenita, and Tanija, were?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Tanija was 12 or 13. She was born in 1980. Dzenita was born in 1986. Sanela was born in 1970 or '71. In 1970 or 1971, something like that. Twenty years old, 17 years old, and Tanija, 13 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sanela, in 1993, did she have a baby?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: In -- she had a baby in January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The baby was six months old?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: On the 23rd, I think. Six months old. Not -- not even a full six months old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, in 1992 and 1993, were you a member of any military organisation?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: No. I was never in a military organisation apart from the JNA. I served my -- I did my military service there. But in 1993, no. In 1992, I did transport troops on two occasions when there were these Serbs in this area. Then they withdrew. Apparently there were clashes, then there was withdrawal in the direction of Stolac, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: May I stop you there. Is it correct, then, that because you were a haulier with your own truck that you, in 1992, assisted in transporting troops with your truck? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes. They knew I had this, so on two occasions the beginning I transported them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: For which army is this? I'm sorry if I interrupt. For which army?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: At the time it was the HVO, because that part was under the command of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did you yourself have any uniform or weapons?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Later I spent some time on guard in the command, but I did shift work and I was a civilian. But when they were preparing trenches, I was called there during that period, and I was also asked to fell these trees in order to protect the trenches. This was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This was also for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, your main activity during that period, 1992 to 1993, was that, as you mentioned at the beginning to Your Honours, that you were involved in agricultural work, telling your own soil?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992 we could still till the land. We worked as usual, and in 1993, up until about June. Yes, until about -- well, in June the situation became insecure and what happened, happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just before coming to June, July, 1993, into 1992 the -- is it correct that in the area where you lived the ethnic composition was mixed although the majority of people there were of?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as the Dubrava plateau is concerned, the Capljina and Stolac municipality, there were people who regardless of their ethnicity -- well, yes, I think that was the case in Dubrava. From Recice, Dubravica, up in Masline, Borovi, et cetera, Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: But it might not be the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you very briefly tell the Court or give the Court an idea of what the relationship between the inhabitants, the different ethnic groupings was in 1992 in the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1992, it was in April, mid-April, and that's when the war broke out more or less, at the beginning of April. And on the first day I had taken some land from a neighbour. We cooperated. My mother was in a poor condition. His brother was from Belgrade. He was a doctor. And then a day or two before I took this person to Trebinje. There were check-points and there were troops up in the Serbian part, and then on the following day I took this person to Ploce, and I returned about noon, let's say, or about 11.00. There must have been a bus at 9.00 from Ploce. It doesn't really matter. When I arrived in Capljina, I was that the war had already started. What should I do, go home? I said I'll try to do so. I returned home immediately on that day. I used the main road. Check-points had been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The war that you're referring to is the outbreak of the conflict with the Serbs in 1992 on the Dubrava plateau; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: At the Dubrava plateau there were these troops, tanks, anti-armour vehicles. They were there with their weapons, but people passed through, et cetera. I suppose this was a kind of preparation, but -- I can't remember the exact date, but it was in April, 1992 that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: May I interrupt you again? I will ask you a specific question on this: When this conflict broke out, was there any instance where you as a result of the relationship you had with Croat neighbours gave assistance to your Croat neighbours? Could you briefly tell the Court about that if it happened?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: At that moment -- well, I came home, and since the shells had already started falling around the houses, I crossed the Neretva. I couldn't go by car. I left my car on the left bank, and we crossed over in a boat. Well, I won't mention all the details, but I came back the next day, whereas other people stayed over there, some Croats, too, and Muslims, Bosniaks. Some were there more, some were less. Some people were successful, others weren't. But I returned the following day, and I said I could help somebody if they stayed there. And that was the second day. I went to Ploce that day. Then I came home and returned to my family. They were in Opuzen. And then in the evening we went to Ploce, to Croatia. I was there for about two weeks because there were no conflicts. More people stayed and many people were going back because of their cattle, because of their livestock. People went back because the animals were left on their own. So they went back to feed the cattle. And I returned myself, but not for long, with my family, and I followed -- I was ordered -- well, the children and the elderly, and my mother was killed across the Neretva River on that occasion. But I was still at home. I managed to get my mother and children across the Neretva, linked to Medjugorje. It's up at Surmanci hill up there. They were born there. One was from that house and my mother was from another house on that side. That's what happened, I didn't know when she was killed, when she died up there when the army withdrew three days before. Anyway, it was a shell that killed two elderly women, a neighbour and my mother. And we learnt about this when they had withdrawn, when -- the HVO and the army and the Muslims. This was all formed together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: At this point, I'd like to ask you just once again, now that you've given the background as to the situation that pertained there, did you receive any specific request regarding the safety or security of any of your Croat neighbours, and what did you do?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: How do you mean specific request? There was no need -- well, he was my neighbour. He was -- he was there, had a house just like me. And later on when I took the woman away, after this sort of duel across the river Neretva, this person who was a Croat, and her daughter had come from Belgrade, and I took her to Pula to be with her son. And at the Domanovici check-point, I took her there, and she went to Belgrade after that. And -- well, this wasn't in 1993. It was in 1992, the beginning of May -- April, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: This lady that you refer to whom you transported to Pula, was she a Croatian?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: She was a Croat, yes. Yes. She was Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And how far is Pula from Recice?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: About 700, 500. It's towards the border with Italy. So it took me the whole night. It's a long way away, and it was night-time, and you have to go through Zadar, Sibenik, because I couldn't get the boat. I didn't take the ferry. But we managed to cross over and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So, sir, if I may sum up from this, or if I am permitted to make -- or put something to you, if you were prepared to transport this lady so far, were the relations between you and your Croat neighbours good?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: At that time, yes, they were still good, but later on, mostly in 1993 -- I don't know. I don't know how this all came about, when the conflicts --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that in a moment. Sir, just before getting there, during 1992 and the first part of 1993, did the HVO establish any positions or posts or barracks in Domanovici?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can say that straight away that's what I heard and that's what I saw as well, I was born there, of course, so I had to communicate and work and -- yes, I understood them to say that there was an Intervention Platoon in the school, and later on in the barracks. Well, I didn't go there. I wasn't interested in that. But they used to call it an Intervention Platoon, and you could see soldiers. And then of course in 1993, in July, and even before the 1st, from Gubavica and certain areas, people were being arrested. And where we were in our own village, in our little hamlet, you didn't dare appear if you were a Muslim. They would -- if you went to market, they'd take your car and all the goods you were carrying. They took the people prisoner. So we didn't dare go outside and be seen after the 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If you say they took your car, they arrested you, who are you referring to as "they"?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't at that point in time, but the other people a few days before the 1st of July or on the 1st of July, and then the 1st and 2nd of July, people who were at the market, for example, might have been taking their trucks with their goods there but they would leave them because they might have heard about it and then they would leave their vehicles and go. And my car and my truck stayed behind when I was taken to the camp, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could I ask you just again, but who was arresting these people or taking their vehicles?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: At that time it was the HVO who were the army who was -- they were the soldiers and the authority in Capljina. I think it was the HVO and Croatia, because before that, in June, I had registered my car. I took my driving licence, took out this Croatian insurance, and they just gave me a piece of paper where it said Herceg-Bosna. The stamp said Herceg-Bosna. And they took my driving licence away and exchanged this piece of paper for my driving licence, and they took the original for the car that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So let's turn to the arrests that you referred to at the beginning of July. Can you tell us at the beginning of July whether men in your area, Domanovici and Recice, were also arrested, or what happened?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, Dubravska Visoravan, from Stole, Capljina. There were quite a lot of soldiers. There were some relations of mine and neighbours from neighbouring villages that I came across in the camp. They were in the HVO, whether at the check-point or in the trench, or they -- they were collected up and taken to the camps, and some of them still wearing those camouflage uniforms. And if they didn't have anything to wear they would give them the olive-green uniforms in exchange for those HVO insignia and things. And there were a lot like that. I'm sure they'll come and -- here and speak to you. I know about my relatives. Some were even beaten up. One of them from Dretelj. He was beaten up on the first and second day, but most of them remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, were you arrested on the 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: They arrested me when I -- on the 13th of July or, rather, the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Before the 14th of July. At the beginning of July, were you arrested then?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the -- of July they came to look for me twice. On one occasion I was digging up potatoes in the backyard for the winter or I don't know what I was doing, getting ready for the winter, getting food for the winter. Doesn't matter. Then my wife noticed them, and I thought the -- it was the neighbour's car. And the president of the Croatian Community in that place, Jozo Popovic or his son, he had a car, a yellow Golf, and the soldiers didn't know about me or my house without somebody from my village telling them, a neighbour whatever. Anyway, they came by and my wife warned me when she saw them coming from the opposite direction. They had come previously, but I wasn't at home. And she thought it was probably they'd come about the same business. So she told me, she warned me, and I hid in the shed 20 or 30 metres away from the house. I had two cows in the shed and some hay. There was another relative of mine, so he we hid together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And you didn't find you or arrest you at that occasion?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Not then. They didn't find us because we hid in the hay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, those men who came, and if I heard correctly, you mentioned they were HVO soldiers. Is that correct? Or HVO members?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: That is correct, 100 per cent correct. There were no other soldiers. Now, there couldn't have been anybody else who came. It couldn't have been anybody else. They came with weapons. They were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, how did you recognise these men as being HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, by the insignia they had. They had insignia on their arms, on their sleeves. And I knew the car, too. I knew who drove the car. My wife knew who the driver of the car was too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, is it correct that soldiers came a second time to look for you but at that occasion you were not at home, you were away, and that's how you escaped at that time or arrest at that time?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I wasn't at home that time. Anyway, they came twice, at least twice looking for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of July until perhaps the 10th, because on the 13th what happened, happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, between the beginning of July and until the 13th of July, is it correct that apart from that one time when you were away you mostly stayed at home and inside?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: At home or round about my neighbour's home.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please. Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Kruger, and also the witness started to speak. I would like only to ask the following question: In the statement made by the witness earlier, page 1, about the middle of the page he speaks about -- about those soldiers in the beginning of July, 1993, who were dressed in camouflage uniforms, and they came, as they put it then, "to look for me on two occasions." And then he continues quoting you to say -- the witness said and wrote that: "The soldiers would come to look for the Muslims they knew were still in their houses." And then he continued to say that, "I can day that those soldiers were members of HVO or HV. I cannot claim," he continued, "that all of them were Croats. Maybe some soldiers were of other nationalities." End of the quotation from the statement. So my question is to the -- to the witness, to Mr. Hasic, if -- he saw soldiers coming to collect Muslim persons at that time, if they belonged to HVO or HV or, as he mentioned, that maybe they were of some other nationalities, that is, not Croats. If he would be able to tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They might not have been Croats. They might have been Hungarians or Muslims, but they were the HVO and authorities, Capljina, Dubravska, that area, the Dubrava plateau. Or it could have been the Croatian army. I don't know. I didn't follow all these things. But when my neighbour was taken away, they came in a car, in a bus, took had him away. But when they came looking for me I saw that two of the men were armed, and I could see him although I was hidden in the shed. Their truck was near -- the truck was nearby. They came into the -- I can say that they were HVO and that they were in uniform and that they were armed. Now, there might have been Muslims or Bosniaks together with the HVO but under their command. They were the same. They were with them. If they were good, they were good. If they were bad, they were bad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, on the day before the 13th of July, in addition to the HVO positions that you mentioned were at the school and at the barracks in Domanovici, did you see any other soldiers or movements of soldiers? That's the 12th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the barracks there were even tanks -- or, before July, I went to Capljina. Before July, I would see a tank and I would see people from over there. I knew a neighbour of mine. His father was a Macedonian, but he was born there, and his wife. I saw him as a soldier. The other's now gone to Germany, but I saw them going out of the barracks. This is a hospital. And then -- well, on the 12th, in the afternoon, I personally saw a VBR, multiple-rocket launcher, or like a jeep with weapons, towards Mostar. And then the road is leads on to Dubrovnik, Mostar-Dubrovnik-Sarajevo. It's a hundred yards from my home. But they were on their way to Gubavica and they were on their way to Mostar with the weapons. There were two or three military vehicles. On the 13th the event we mentioned happened, fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: May I -- let's turn to the 13th. On the 13th, in addition to the HVO positions at the barracks and at the school, was any other position occupied on that day by the HVO in Recice or close to your house?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. That morning in the -- around the houses my neighbours, good neighbours, we cooperated, and still today we say hello, we greet each other, and if any of us needs help we help each other out. I saw -- it's rather a large property and stretches down towards the barracks. I saw two Buntici, and underneath the peach trees, the peach orchard, and -- my neighbour Buntic, it was the Buntic household. From the orchard I saw several soldiers rushing out in front of Mate Buntic's house. They rushed out with rucksacks and weapons and their camouflage uniform. And there was a house close by there where I used to -- well, his -- my neighbour's sister was there building her house. They started building it before the war, and I would help out sometimes, too. And there was a sort of point of defence there. They concentrated themselves there. Maybe they were in the houses too. But they were in that area, and I saw them arrive, and I saw their rucksacks and weapons. They were wearing military uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And which -- which army did these men belong to?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, none other than the HVO. I don't know. Perhaps they might have been from some other area, but it was and ought to have been the HVO in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the assistance of the usher, I would like to show the witness on the ELMO a -- a rough map. Now, this map or sketch was circulated this morning to Your Honours and to the Defence, and I trust if there are no objections this may facilitate the understanding of the following portion of the witness's evidence. The rough sketch was produced by the witness, and I re-drew it without the markings and propose that the witness now make some markings on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recognise this drawing as the drawing that you and I discussed yesterday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The road towards Mostar coming from Capljina, then the road towards Stolac. Yes. This -- that's the Mostar road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, is this a very, very rough and incomplete representation of Domanovici and Recice?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not complete, but roughly speaking, yes, that's where the barracks were. It shows the general distance of the school, the Domanovici junction or crossroads, and my neighbours house, the Buntic neighbours. That's roughly what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, if you could take a pen, and if you could look on the device next to you where the usher will show you, I want to ask you to mark with an A where your house is or what represents your house on this picture.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: This one here. A. A. I can put the A right on the house. Or I'll put it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you mark with a B the school in Domanovici where HVO were situated.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: That's the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And with a C, if you could mark the barracks where the HVO were also situated.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: A "C" you want? Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, the house which you just described before I showed you this map where you saw soldiers move to on the morning of the 13th, if you can mark that with a D.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: These are the four houses, one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you mark with an X the approximate spot where your daughters were shot. We will be getting to this evidence in a moment. Perhaps, sir, if I could ask you another question first. Could you mark with an E the house of Meho Hasic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] E.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes, with an E the house of Meho Hasic.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you could mark with an F the house where the bodies of your daughters were taken on the evening of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: F?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: With an F, yes.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. I notice that you have drawn a further block. Could you tell the Court what that block indicates?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, since there's this house next to the house where the children were, but perhaps there was no one in this house. But there is a house here. The distance between the two houses is about five metres, so it was just to help me find my bearings. There's Rafo Popovic's house to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you now, if you're oriented, if you could indicate with an X the approximate place or spot where your two daughters were shot.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's about a hundred or a hundred and fifty metres from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll come back to this aspect in a bit. At this stage I would like you to tell the Court in your own words about what happened on the 13th of July, that day, with regard to your daughters.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: I was at home. I woke up in the morning early. It was July, in the summer. I spoke about 5.00, and I heard something like an explosion. It was a shell, perhaps, or bursts of fire. It came from behind the hill, above the hill. The hill's about a kilometre away from where I was. You could hear these -- these explosions early in the morning. And I was at home, and at about 10.00 I was walking around the house, and below a fig tree there was a vineyard, an even at that point in time, well, I felt a hissing noise in the air, and you could hear a shot as if someone had opened fire from a weapon with a silencer, but I didn't know where from. But I've heard these explosions, the sound of sniper fire, but a silencer was used and you didn't know where the shot had been fired from. So perhaps I didn't react immediately. But nothing happened after that. About noon, in the afternoon -- it was afternoon. It didn't really matter. I went to where my children were, where my children were killed later. I went to a neighbour's to see what was the situation was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Which neighbour did you go to?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, my neighbour Hajro. And there was this person Popovic. I even found Meho in the house. And there were two other neighbours who were little -- who live a little further away but they're in Recice. Perhaps they were a kilometre and a half from Recice, in fact. They were also from Recice but from the Krc hamlet. And then I heard that they had brought them there. Some Muslim in the armija. I don't know whether there was someone else, though, but there were only these two Croats whom I knew there. One was older than me, two or three years older than me, and the other one was younger. I knew them. They were on their own, and the owner of the house told me that they had been brought there, but this person had left. I didn't come across the soldier who was a member of the armija, or perhaps there were several of them, I don't know. And then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I may stop you at this point. On that morning were you personally aware of any armija units or armija soldiers or non-HVO army personnel in Domanovici-Recice?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: In Domanovici, no, I'm not aware of that. But since there was fighting up there, there was the Grbavica hill which links up to Mostar, they went to Grbavica. I suppose there were army check-points there. So the armija was probably there. There was fighting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Domanovici and Recice?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: In Domanovici, Recice, I personally don't know about that. I didn't see anyone, but I can't claim that there was no one. But in this area, then I could control. In the area where my daughters were killed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to repeat the last part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, could you perhaps repeat the last part of your sentence, please. The interpreters did not hear that, of your last sentence. You were saying, "In Domanovici and Recice I personally don't know about that. I didn't see anyone, but I can't claim that there was no one. But in this area, then I could control. In the area where my daughters were killed ..."

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Where we were, this region, it's the Glavica hamlet. And the area where these neighbour's houses are and where the check-point is, in that area at that time you couldn't see any troops, at least not in that part. In the area between our houses. In the area between the place where my daughters were killed and this other part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to check something, whether you said that on that day, on the 13th of July, there was no fighting from the morning onwards. You said that there were no armija soldiers in the surroundings but that you had heard an explosion and, according to you, it could have been snipers. There was no fighting. There were no attacks launched in the village. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no fighting, there were no troops, but in the morning I heard fighting but in the neighbouring village which is about two kilometres away. It's at an elevation. There's a hill, a mountain. It was a neighbouring hill. You couldn't see anything. You could just hear the sound of fighting. There was perhaps fighting in the course of the day there. But in this area up to Domanovici there was just sniper fire. You could hear sniper shots. And when I was at my neighbour's, they said that a bullet or two had been fired and had hit something in Meho's bathroom, but there were no troops that you could see in that area, and there was no fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we have to stir up very painful memories for you, but we need information about the death of your daughters. If I have understood you correctly, you were at a neighbour's. At what time exactly were you informed of the fact that your two daughters had been shot at? At what time were you informed of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Naturally I know when. I was observing the scene from my house, and when I arrived at the neighbour's, that was in the afternoon. I don't know when exactly. It was in the summer. It wasn't night, but it was around 6.00 in the afternoon. As I have said, perhaps it's because there were two elderly people, two elderly neighbours who were sick, and they arrived there, and there were the children in the house. They were impatient. They were being helped. And the children then wanted to go to where we previously had a house at Glavica. It was 500 metres away. They had others they knew there. It was a little further away from the road. They asked me whether they could go there. I said they could but that they should be careful because shots had already been fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have to put very precise questions to you because it's necessary to know what happened exactly. You said that you were informed between 5.00 and 6.00 p.m. Did you go to the site immediately or were you daughters taken elsewhere? Can you provide us with any information about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went there immediately. When they left the house, they went through the house and through the vineyard and orchard the road was 50 metres from my house. There were these peach trees and there were the vines, and then they got to the asphalt road. They went further on to my property, 50 or 70 metres away, and that area was visible because there was this orchard in the other area. And the area wasn't very visible. When they came out into the open, almost next to the houses, when they reached the road there's a slight elevation towards Glavica, and there's a little bridge there, a canal. That's where they were passing by. My wife was in front of them, and the three of them were behind her. They were holding on to each other, and they could be seen. They were wearing these tracksuits which were red or pink, but they were visible. And I heard the shots and cries for help, because that was about a hundred, a hundred and twenty metres as the crow flies from my house. And then within a minute or two I ran through the orchard and vineyard to see what had happened. I arrived there, and when I arrived there my middle daughter had already died. And then I saw my older daughter. I was told by my wife, "Dzenita has been wounded." I returned home and then returned back to where Sanela was. She was in the ditch. She must have jumped into the ditch or fallen into the ditch, and she couldn't say anything. And I return, and I said, "Shall we get you out of there?" She said, "Yes." And when she said that, I picked her up. I saw she was bleeding. There was a wound to the left of her heart, and she was bleeding from there. And at that point she -- she died. I was crying for about five minutes. Rafo's wife Katica arrived first. She was the godmother to one of my daughters. And there was some sort of a car nearby, and she was kneeling behind the car and crying. And I was in the ditch, in the canal. And when things had calmed down a bit, when night had fallen, we took them away into the house belonging to the Hasic family. He was a cousin of my grandfather's. We left them in the cellar there. And in the evening we went over to Meho's house because he had a bigger basement. And there were a number of people there and that's where we spent the night. We stayed until morning. I can continue if you like and tell you what happened next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, apart from your two daughters, on that day no one else was shot at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in that area. No one in that area. I won't know whether anyone was shot at in the surroundings, but in our hamlet, as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When your daughter died in your arms, after she had died in your arms did you examine the wounds? You said that the person -- that the daughter who spoke to you just before she died had a wound at the level of her heart that was bleeding. Did you have a look at this one or not? Did you examine it closely or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a good look at it. When I picked her up, I had a good look. The other daughter was hit in the back of the head. She had a very swollen eye, but she was hit in the back of her head. And when an exhumation was performed about five years later in 1993 -- 1998, I recognised her when I had a look at the wound to her head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you'll have a 20-minute break now, and we will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor back to you, Mr. Kruger, Mr. Mundis I believe there is something you would like to inform us of, but would you like to do that in the present of the witness or shall we ask the witness to least courtroom temporarily?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I think I can do it in such a way that we don't need to ask the witness to -- to be escorted out of the courtroom. Shortly before the last break I received an e-mail concerning the scheduling for the remainder of this week and the witnesses that are scheduled to appear. As perhaps some of the Defence teams know and as I informed the Chamber's legal officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would also like to have a follow-up question. Mr. Hasic mentioned before the break answering my question that -- when I asked him about the soldiers coming in early July to pick up mainly Muslim men, et cetera, he mentioned that among the soldiers in his view there were also Hungarians. I checked the transcript and he mentioned and spoke about Hungarians. Given the fact that I am also from Hungary, I would like to ask you two questions. The first, why did you think that they were Hungarians? If you probably listen to their talk, or if you know some Hungarian words. And second, what kind of uniforms they were dressed in and wore in that case. So were they in the HVO or any other uniforms when you have seen them, or you may have heard about their being there during that particular time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, Judge. Hungary Germany, Bulgaria. I apologise; it wasn't intentional. That's why I"perhaps," "who knows." They were from all parts from there, from here. It was wartime. Like the Germans and -- I didn't hear them talking or anything like that, I just sort of said, "soldiers wearing HVO uniforms," because the HVO was there. That's what I meant. I didn't actually mean -- well, the Hungarians, another nation, whether they were there or I heard them, that they were there, it was just the HVO uniform. It's not that I heard them close to or see them who came to get me or -- or those who came to get me or the houses. Well, it was the HVO soldiers there. Their command was there. So that's -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, but if you said that among the HVO soldiers who by definition were the inhabitants of your country that there were foreigners, it's something when -- is it something that you heard on the radio or on television, something like that, or is that a fact that you yourself noted and observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not according to my own experience. It was just following -- well, not following. You hear about things. They said the Mujahedin or people from Germany or the Foreign Legion or -- I didn't really follow these things. I didn't know about them. But I said possibly, you know. But all I know is -- for a fact is that it was the HVO soldiers and their command. I said that it could have been other people, too. There might have been Bosniaks the HVO, as indeed there were. Perhaps there were good ones, bad ones, those for their people, against their people. But that I saw them personally or I had experience of them or that I was in the conflict, I was not, but there were cases on the basis of what I heard, what other people said, the media, things like that. I personally didn't see them, no, or hear anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I would like to be of assistance to the witness and explain what this was about. The question referred to the Croats who had done something, and the witness wanted to tell us that that was done by the HVO. Now, whether in those HVO units there were Croats, Muslim, Hungarians, or whoever else other is not important, that what was important was that they were the HVO. So perhaps my explanation can be of assistant and the witness can confirm it or not. And I'd be very pleased if I could help the Court out on this point and clarify the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try and clarify it. As far as I know, the HVO -- it was the HVO authority and the HVO soldiers, and whether it was Herceg-Bosna or whatever, but the main -- the main army, the main army and soldiers were the HVO when the war began in our area. So it should have been the HVO. Now, whether there were any others there -- anyway, they were Croat soldiers. When I say the HVO, the Croatian soldiers were the majority, and the HVO authority, Croatian authority, or the authority of Herceg-Bosna or whatever was decided at that time. What they wanted, I don't really know. I'm not well-versed in things like that, but that's how it was. That's how it should have been. Now, whether there were any other people in the army, I can't claim. I don't want to claim anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, sir, you said that they were in a house, that they had put up in a house. Now, on the basis of what you had seen, these HVO soldiers, how many of them were there? Can you give us a figure, a general figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many of them in the house. Well, they might have come before evening fell, I don't know. But in the morning, the next day, the next morning, when you could hear the shooting and when all this was going on in the hills and there was this explosion, I walked round the house and just by chance I happened to look across the road to the neighbours' houses. And I said that at about 10.00 the shot came from there. Without knowing -- well, you could hear sort of muffled shots in the air. I saw about three soldiers rushing out at that point, running out of the vineyard in front of the house and the other two or three houses there. And then they entered that half -- semi-finished house. Whether there were any others there I can't say. I wasn't close by. But I saw the soldiers come there with their weapons, whether it was an automatic rifle or whatever, and with their rucksacks and camouflage uniform, and they were rushing out of the vineyard. So it wasn't intentional. I just happened to look that way and that's what I saw with my very own eyes when I happened to look that way. And I assume that that was how my daughters were killed. Maybe when this bullet went whizzing by my ear and I felt -- I saw this or felt the shots being shot in the air, I should have maybe done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Now, there's something that might cause confusion in our minds. You said that it was 10.00 in the morning. Now, we understood it that your daughter was -- was killed -- your daughters were killed between 5.00 and 6.00 in the afternoon. So when you saw these soldiers running out of the vineyard, what time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in the morning, perhaps 6.00 or 7.00, when they were coming from the vineyard. I was round the house --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But when they came out -- running out of the vineyard, is that the moment you heard shots, gunshots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not then, no. No, no, no. Not shots in the air then, no. That's not what I said. That's not what I meant. But the shoot -- the shooting in the morning at 5.00 in the neighbouring village, and one or two hours later was when I saw these people coming out of the vineyard. But the shooting in the neighbouring village was earlier on, and my daughters were killed in the evening. And I said when this bullet whizzed past my ear with this muffled sound from a muffled rifle, I just heard this noise and shots in the air, several shots in the air. Not often, but with the silencers, these shots from the silencers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The morning, the three -- in the morning, the three soldiers that rushed out, were they coming from the neighbouring village where the conflict was taking place and where there was shooting? So in your opinion, these three soldiers, were they coming from the neighbouring village?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I hesitate to -- to register a small point, but the phrase "in your opinion," we do respectfully suggest the question is better phrased without that because we are as Your Honour indicated at the very beginning before this witness gave evidence trying to draw a clear distinction between what this witness actually knows, observed, and can say, and opinion which then shades into speculation. And that phrase does carry that risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stewart. You're observation seems to be entirely misplaced. I took all caution to ask him where the three soldiers who were running had come from. They didn't parachute down into the area. They had to come from somewhere, and I was asking him where they were coming from, whether from the neighbouring village or could they have come from somewhere else. It's the witness who is going to tell us about that, if he knows. Do you understand the problem, Witness? You saw three soldiers rushing out of the vineyard. Where could they have come from? Do you have an explanation or none? Or because you said that in -- at 5.00 in the morning you heard shots in the neighbouring village, the next-door village, so it would be logical to assume that those three men had come from the neighbouring village. Witness, could you tell us about that? Do you know, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can tell you exactly. The distance from the barracks is about 300 metres, and they came from the barracks. They couldn't have come from anywhere else. And they had a check-point there where they were stationed. Perhaps they had reinforcements. There were probably more people there because there were preparations on the day before, and I saw them going towards Mostar and Gubavica. So these were probably reinforcements sent from the barracks because there were orchards there, vineyards there, no settlements there. So they were coming right from the barracks, which were opposite my house at a distance of 300 and 400 metres, and you could see that area. So they came directly through the orchards and the vineyard and came up onto the houses from the vineyards, not from the opposite direction where there was the shooting. I couldn't have seen them, because there's a wood there. So I couldn't have seen them if they had come from that side like I saw these people, because it's visible. You could see from the barracks. And I just happened to look and see them. They had weapons. They had these rucksacks and camouflage uniforms. Perhaps they were -- well, they were probably reinforcements, and the that's the only area that the shots could have come from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't know where these three men came from. They might have been reinforcements, but that's a supposition, a hypothesis; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the barracks. I know that. They couldn't have come from anywhere else. It must have been from the barracks. There was nothing else there. The barracks or Domanovici, but the barracks are there and that's where they must have come from. There's nothing -- no other way they could have come from. Not from the neighbouring village where the fighting was going on but from the barracks. I couldn't have seen them had they come from the neighbouring village, but I saw them because they came from the direction of the barracks. I could see that side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was a question from the Bench. No. You seem to have answered the question. Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, just a few more things. Your youngest daughter, Tanija, was she injured in any way during this incident?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, she was wounded, too, at the same time. She was hit in the knee, her left knee, and she was operated later on in Germany. But she spent the night there, and I took her to get assistance for her to the soldiers, the HVO in Domanovici where they were. They were put up in a cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was that the next morning?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that was the next morning when I took her there in order to get assistance. And then I went to get the coffins for my other two daughters, and then I went home to drive the coffins there with Rafo Popovic because I couldn't do that myself. I did have a truck, but I couldn't do it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, at the point where you took your daughter for assistance at the HVO in Domanovici, can you give the Court an idea of how many soldiers there were there that morning on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: For emergencies, first aid, in that coffee bar. But I return, and there were already soldiers at this crossroads. I knew some of my neighbours there, and they were sort of reinforcements or something like that. There were about 50 or 100 of them, soldiers, at that -- at those crossroads. They were on foot. They were wearing military uniforms. They were armed that morning. After the 13th that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could return back to the rough sketch which is on the ELMO next to you. Do you see the crossroads where you saw these soldiers that morning on this sketch?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. The junction is from Capljina, then Stolac, then Mostar. That crossroads. The coffee bar is here. That's where the coffee bar is, right up at the crossroads, and then Capljina is over there. There's a bend towards Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you mark the crossroads that you've just indicated with a G, please.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir -- and you may turn this picture around as you please to or general yourself. You've indicated your house as A. You've indicated the house of Meho Bukmam -- sorry, my apologies, Meho Hasic as an E. Could you indicate with an X where that bridge is where Dzenita and Sanela were shot, please. On the paper next to you on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to tender this as an In Court Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Mr. Kruger. I'm a bit lost. I thought that his daughters were hit at the level of the crossroads, and now he seems to have indicated another area. So can we go back to that and be -- receive more precise information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us the place where your daughters were shot, where is that in relation to your house and the house of Meho Bukman -- I'm sorry, Meho Hasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Hasic, it would be good if you were to draw the way your daughters went from your house as a line. Did they go right or did they go left when they came to the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My house is here. That's the main road, and they went this way. Those are the houses. There's an underpass here, and then you come to these three houses. And it was by this middle house that I took my two daughters into from here. So from my entrance you go on the road. You go -- take the road this way until you reach those first houses here. It's about a hundred, a hundred and twenty metres. Well, about a hundred metres. It's not important. But anyway, from the road. Fifty metres from my house to the road and then down the road to this spot here. And that's the crossroads. This is Domanovici. Maybe I made some other markings, but this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you show us where the coffee bar was? Could you show the spot where the coffee bar was? Place a cross there or a letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's it. That's the coffee bar, coffee shop. Right by the crossroads, on the right-hand side. Right up by the crossroads. Should I put a letter, a K? Let's put a K for kafana, cafe. That's where the first HVO point was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, you've shown us where the sniper was. Could you show us where the sniper was again and where your three daughters were, because in fact your three daughters were there. You said Tanija was wounded in the knee. So can you show us what direction the shot took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the crossroads at Domanovici. They should be -- this is my house and how you get to the road from my house. This isn't the proper sketch for -- because my house was opposite here, and that's the road, and this is the road. They were here. I've already marked that. The houses, and that's my house. That's opposite. So that would be the direction, from these two houses. Two houses are habitable. People live in them. They've been fully constructed. The other house was still under construction. But it's all within a space of 10 or 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment ago we learnt that your third daughter was hit in the knee. She was wounded in the knee. By a shot, a bullet wound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, certainly, yes, a bullet, because all three of them were walking together, walking towards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, did they take the bullet out of her knee? Was the bullet taken out of her knee? Because you said that she was taken to the first aid HVO post apparently, and I understood it that she was later on operated on in Germany. Who operated your daughter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the bullet was not lodged in the knee. It was just her tendon that was damaged. And in Zagreb, a certain time later, she went to see a doctor. But since it was wartime, she couldn't go on time. She went when she could. She was transferred from -- to Capljina first and then from Capljina to Zagreb and then she returned. But that bullet wasn't lodged in the knee. It just wounded her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your last daughter, the third, the bullet that wounded your daughter -- did your daughter tell you what happened? Did she say, "Well, all three of us were walking along the road"? Did she tell you how it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was all clear. When they left the house, I followed them with my eyes. I could see them go out onto the road and then walk down the road. Their mother was there, my wife, with her granddaughter, two, three, or four metres in front, and my daughters were behind. And when they came to this open space, they were watching, too, and that's when they were killed and wounded, Your Honour. I saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I understand you correctly, you saw your three daughters as they walked along the road. Your wife was there with the six-month old granddaughter, and it was at that point in time that your three daughters were wounded by bullets. But you just heard the whizzing of shots, because you didn't hear any explosions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were shots in the air as if you were using a silencer. They were muffled sounds. You couldn't make out exactly where they were coming from, and I think they must have used a silencer. But there was no other place. You could see these -- that's where the soldiers were seen. So there were shots. And probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to ask you about Gabela. Just one final we on this, and that is what were your daughters and your wife wearing? How were they dressed at the time of this incident?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: I can tell you what my daughters were wearing. I don't -- well, normal women's clothing. I think they were wearing tracksuits, my two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: And my middle daughter, she was a little -- she had red on. She was wearing a red tracksuit, and she was a little taller. So you could see it, but it was all civilian clothing. What more can I tell you? It was light coloured, coloured civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, the next day, the 14th of July, you had already told the Court that you went to buy coffins or get coffins in Capljina. Is it correct that you were prevented from returning to your village because you were then taken to Gabela? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: That's correct. There's proof that I was in camp. The Red Cross can prove this. I perhaps have already said this. I set off with a Croatian neighbour because I could do so. I arrived down there and the imam in Capljina gave me these coffins, because the shop in which I wanted to buy the coffins was shut. The imam, whose name is also Hasan, he died after the war. I don't think he was killed. He was younger than me. And he gave me those things. And then I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may interrupt you. I'm afraid we'll have to cut out some of the detail at this stage. Were you taken, before going to Gabela, on that morning to the police station in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I had taken the things from the imam, I set off, said I could inscribe the names of my children. I set off to Capljina, to Trebisac [phoen] which is where the salesman was from. I went there with my neighbour, and we found him there. He said we could come immediately. We went before him in our car. We waited in front of the shop on the road in the town of Capljina. I saw him. I knew this neighbour. I assume that this neighbour whose house was about 5 or 600 metres from mine, I assume he saw me and he informed the police, because the salesman hadn't arrived by that time. And they took down my particulars and those of Rafo Popovic. It was the military police, I assume. They were in military uniform. I then went to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Of which organisation the military police?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, of the HVO army. They looked like the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did they then take you to the -- to the police station in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they took me to the police station, to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And whom did you talk to at the police station?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: We met Rafo Popovic and his cousin, Velimir, the son of Karlo. Rafo was born in the same village I was born in. He died after the war. At the time he was alive. But his son was the deputy of the police commander, and he said they should take me to the Gabela camp. I said my children it been killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Yes. And what was his reaction when you said your children had been killed?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: He told me that Croats were dying too. He said he knew nothing. "You have to go to the Gabela camp. Rafo will be responsible for burying your children." And then I gave my details to a woman in the police station, and then the policeman took me to Gabela because it's perhaps 5 or 700 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, if I may ask you from that point. You arrived at Gabela, and is it correct that at Gabela you indicated that you wanted to be released so that you could go and bury your daughters? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was encouraged because I knew the man. Before the war he was also the police commander. I knew him. And given my work as a haulier --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphones are switched off. Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer. The interpreter didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I knew this person at the gate, he was an elderly person, he had already retired even before the war. He took down people's details. He asked me, "What are you doing here?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: May I stop you there. Did he allow you to wait in an area so that somebody could come talk to you later on that same day?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, he helped me to the extent he could. He detained me at the gate. There was a room there, even a few beds. I sat down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And at about 7.00 that evening, who came to see you where you were waiting in that area at the gate?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: I knew him. There was the judge -- he was a judge before the war and now he was in uniform, or on that occasion he arrived in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did he say in what capacity he was there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was there. Naturally they told me. They took me across the road to the canteen. It used to be a military canteen. There were warehouses there, and at that point in time it was a canteen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Who was present at that point in the canteen?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: The camp commander entered the canteen. I didn't know him that well. I knew him as a waiter before the war. They said he was the -- Commander Previsic, Bosko; Boko. And together with an escort this gentleman arrived. He used to work in the technical maintenance company but that's not person. There was an escort in military uniform. They asked me some questions. I -- well, they had come because Mr. Ravnjak wanted to help me, to have me released so that I could bury my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ravnjak, was that the person at the gate whom you met when you arrived at Gabela?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's Ravnjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you tell or did you ask the judge or tell him that you wanted to be released so that you could go and bury your daughters?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked them to allow me to bury them. We spoke to each other. I asked them why was the situation such that I couldn't even bury my children. We had been on good terms with our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What was his reaction or response?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, it was Boko, in fact, who said that I was praising our relationship so that they would let me go, and he said, "You're not normal people." He said he couldn't let me go. There were other harsh words. And then the judge also said -- Katic said that they couldn't let me go. And then they said I should go to the hangar. And that conversation lasted for 10 or 15 minutes, and then I left. There was nothing else to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: During this conversation, this judge whom you've named as Katic, did he inquire about the circumstances of how your daughters had died?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, but since there was this relative of mine, the son of Haso Ramic, and it was after the beginning of the conflict with the Serbs, he'd been part of the authorities in Capljina together with the Croats, and he told me that Ramiz was responsible for the conflict, asked me where he was. I said I didn't know. I said I didn't know where he was. He was hiding around the houses just like me. I know he wasn't in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, before moving on from here, to your knowledge has there ever been any investigation by the HVO into the circumstances surrounding how your daughters were killed?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Sir, no one ever informed me or tried to tell me anything. Earlier on I didn't even make any attempts. Recently they've asked for certain information about civilian victims. So I went to obtain a death certificate. I obtained it, but it says that they died -- they were killed in the municipality of Tasic, about 70 kilometres away from the house. The official knows that's not correct, but that's what the police told them. That's what was written down so that this could be covered up so it wouldn't be possible to say that something happened here or there or such. But no one informed me of anything up until this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said that after this conversation you were then taken into Gabela. Is it correct that you were taken to hangar number 2 eventually where you were held?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: How big was this hangar? Could you give an idea of the dimension?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were these two hills there. There were four in which people were kept. We entered hangar number 3. We stayed there briefly. There was a bit of shoving, pushing and shoving. The guards were a little excited. We entered the hangar. At the gate certain people were maltreated. I heard them. I had heard them cursing. There were about 15 or 20 of us who assembled there, and we entered the hangar number 3. And then they briefly took us into hangar number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And in hangar number 2, what did you find inside hangar number 2?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, the hangar was full of people, and there were these pallets in hangar number 2 because it was used as a military warehouse, a warehouse for equipment. There were slightly larger explosive devices. One was a 40 [as interpreted] at the entrance. And then there were these pallets. 90 per cent of the concrete floor had been covered by these pallets, but they were between the pallets and on the pallets, but mostly on the pallets. And until the Red Cross arrived, they didn't remove the pallets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, you said that the hangar was full of people. Could you give the Court an idea of how many, an estimate perhaps of how many people were in this hangar?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't count them myself, but the hangar was about 30 metres long by -- and 10 or 11 metres wide. There were between 500 and 700 people. We would sit there day and night, but it's not as if we counted the number of people. I don't know exactly, but there would be three of us on a pallet with half a blanket. We would lie on these pallet. A pallet is about a meter and 20 centimetres -- 1.20 square metres, that is. So there were about three of us, three people on one pallet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And who were these people who were in this hangar? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, familiar people from Stolac, Capljina, Dubrava, and later people even came from the area close to Mostar, from the Mostar region, people who used to be with the HVO or came from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: So these men, people from HVO and people from their homes, were these both military and civilian male Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: On the whole, civilians and soldiers. There were quite a lot of people from Stolac who had been with the HVO, who had been in the army at the time, around the 1st of July, before the 1st of July, from Rotanje [phoen], Hodovo, Stolac, Posajnici [phoen], people who had been at these lines. There were quite a lot of them from Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Could you give the Court, but as our time is getting very little, could you give a brief idea to the Court of the food that you received in Gabela during the time you were held there, the initial period?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, it would be better not to say anything, but I'll tell you what we received. A loaf of bread not even a kilo. There were 17 people, and we needed to cut it into 17 parts, divide it among 17 people. And perhaps a macaroni, a quarter of a cup. For about 50 days I and all these people in the hangar received only one meal a day until the Red Cross arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Was this meal served or given to you in the hangar?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. We only ate in the hangar. We received the food in the hangar. We didn't go out. It was only possible to go out briefly during the day if you needed to relieve yourself. But people didn't leave for a 50-day period. There were these buckets in the hangars in which we could urinate. It wasn't necessary to defecate because we were hungry and exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, who were the personnel or the guards at Gabela? Could you give the Court an idea of that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: On the whole the guards were Croats. Mature people. Perhaps there were also people of my age. I had been in Germany with some of them. Perhaps I would meet them, see them. It was all good for them when they saw me. One of them even gave me a tin of fish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And so --

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: There were people or guards from Konjic, quite a few of them. I knew some of them. There was one of them in the camp. They looked for him, then they took him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, if I may interrupt you. Could you give the Court a very brief idea of the treatment you received and the detainees received in Gabela?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Briefly, it was inhumane. I can't really say that they beat me up, maltreated me. It's not as if I was put in solitary confinement. But when you spend 50 days there, it exhausts you. And then you have three kilos of bread for 50 days, and sometimes they'd give you water, sometimes they wouldn't. Before I arrived, the prisoners hadn't been given anything for three days, no water, no food. When I arrived, the very same evening we received a tin of goulash, a 400-gram tin of goulash that had to be divided among eight people. And we received a little of bread, and then one meal a day for about 50 days, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were not beaten. Do you know whether anybody else was beaten?
