utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, they beat other people. I saw that myself. There were these people from Konjic who were guards, as I have said, and they were looking for someone. I don't know whether I can remember his surname. It's not important. They were looking for this person from Konjic who worked for the railways, who lived there. They knew him. They were looking for him. He was in our hangar, the hangar I was in, and on one occasion they took him out, and he came back all beaten up, black and blue, groaning. And then there were two others -- two or three other cases in my hangar that I myself witnessed. And later, when people gathered -- well, there were people who were put into solitary confinement. Some were even killed. I can tell you something about two relatives of mine. There was a person who was 10 -- a relative who was 10 years younger than me. He suffered from asthma. He needed to have adequate medication, but he didn't, and he died at the very beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Did he ask the guards or anybody at the camp for medication or tell them about the problem?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. He knew guards from the place. Someone promised him medication, but he wasn't provided with it. It was urgent. He died on the following day, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Moving on, I want to ask you about Bosko Previsic. Can you give the Court the indication of his attitude towards the detainees from your own personal knowledge?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't behave very well. He was rough. On one occasion in the hangar he told some people that they were no good, that they were illiterate, that they weren't people, that they weren't human. That they were balijas. Since there's a valley there between the hangars, between two hills, he said it would be best if we were all buried there. I don't know whether he was normal or not, but that's what he certainly said, and I personally heard him say this in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Sir, just a final question or two on Gabela. You mentioned that the Red Cross came after about 40 or 50 days after you had arrived. Is it correct that after that period you -- all the detainees received two meals per day?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once they had arrived and once we had been registered at least partially -- well, as of that point in time we were provided with two meals. So for the next 50 days after the Red Cross had arrived we received about two meals a day, and later perhaps even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, to conclude and before I quickly show you a few brief documents, regarding your two daughters Sanela and Dzenita, is it correct that they were buried in the garden of your home in Recice initially?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But I wasn't there to bury them. My neighbours were there. My wife remain at home. My neighbours were relatives of mine. Ramiz was at home then. She told me that they were there together and that they had buried them. And then Ramiz and his brother and other relatives, I think, they buried them. That was on the 14th or 15th, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, a year later is it correct that they were exhumed and buried in a different place?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. A commission -- there was a commission, and -- there was a Serb living there married to a Croat. He was part of the commission. And then they were taken to another place. And when they came to my house, these Croatians from Bosnia, from Sarajevo, when he left in 2000, but they came to my house and transferred them to Tasovcici, Modric, near Capljina, to a Partisan cemetery there, whatever. And in 1998 they were exhumed and transported to Mostar. And I came back home from Germany, and that's when we buried them at Recice, Brestovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: If I may quickly turn to documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regards to documents 09747 and 09748, these two documents relate or are -- pertain to documents recording the fact of the deaths of these two daughters, and they are in support of evidence that the witness has provided, and if there is no objection from the Defence I would wish to tender these as exhibits without showing them to the witness at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no objections, Your Honour, and I assume that my colleagues do not as well. But I don't want to speak for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. We support that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and my thanks to my learned colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, there is then only one other document that I wish to show you, and this is document 04822.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And with the assistance of the registry, if we can put up on the e-court page 7 of 10 of the B/C/S version. Your Honours, this is a report by Mr. Mazowiecki, and I would simply wish to refer the witness to paragraph 20 of this report. It is page 4 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you have that on the screen in front of you, the -- do you have on the screen in front of you -- with the assistance of the usher, the --

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, paragraph 20, I'm going to read certain parts of it for you, and this pertains to or is a description of Gabela. "The picture of conditions inside these places of detention is still not complete." I will skip that part. "One former detainee told the Special Rapporteur's field staff that between 2.000 and 3.000 men were held in the two hangars at Gabela at any one time." In your experience is that accurate, from your time in Gabela? Were people kept in only two hangars?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Two hangars. Not only two or -- one on two but three and four, and from Dretelj, whether they were filled straight away, but I know that people came in to the fourth. There were four hangars. And when I was there the three were all full, because some of my neighbours came after me. They were probably hiding in the woods for a few days. But there were four hangars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: What about the estimate of between 2.000 and 3.000? Is that accurate or too high in your experience?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Perhaps in the four hangars that many, but roughly 500 to 700 people to a hangar. Now, I can't tell you exactly whether there were 3.000 or 2.000, but four hangars. Close to that number, yes. Not only in the two. Well, you could get that many people there, but they couldn't spend any length of time, but in four that would be possible. So 1 or 200 more or less or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd just like to ask you to listen to the rest. You can follow it in the B/C/S version. "The daily food ration consisted of 650 grams of bread to be shared between 16 prisoners and a bowl of thin soup. On some occasions they received no food for two or three days consecutively, apparently at times when HVO forces suffered defeats in areas of Central Bosnia." Is this accurate according to your information and experience? Can you comment on it?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived, as I said, that evening, and the others together, they told me -- well, I -- they told me that they hadn't been given water for three consecutive days, or food either. I didn't experience that particular episode. But when we arrived, there was this -- there were these tins of goulash, and there would be one tin of 400 grams for eight people, to be shared amongst eight people. But this thing for the three days, that's what I heard. They told me they had lived through that. But when I arrived, that didn't happen but they told me that had happened before my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: To continue on that, and then we'll finish with this document. "The hangars were almost hermetically sealed and during the summer months prisoners feared they would suffocate. Guards threatened to spray the hangar walls with heavy-caliber machine-gun fire if they knocked to ask for air." Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Boko Previsic and some of the guards, yes, they said that if we tried -- anybody tried to escape that everything was mined, had been mined. And then there were instances when they would come in, and during the perhaps combat or when the fighting was going on they would provoke us and make us lie down on our stomachs, and they would shoot above our heads. They didn't kill us then, kill anybody then, but they instilled fear in us. And in my hangar that's what we had to do. We had to lie down on our stomachs on the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the last thing is, of course, the -- the diagram or the rough map that the witness has been dealing with. The witness has marked additional things on that, and I wonder if we could perhaps just get him to mark those additional things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have an IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit IC 116.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Would you wish me to request the witness to just mark the line of the projectile which hit his women? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Place your name there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Witness, you have marked on the exhibit -- on the diagram. You ever drawn a line from D to the house or to the place marked F. Could you perhaps mark that with a -- a number 1. Anywhere on that line. Yes. That would be good.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And could you sign the diagram in -- in that open area on the bottom -- to the right of that. In that open area. Yes. That's -- where your hand is now is good.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you put today's date, 27/11/2006.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've going to take our 20-minute break now, and then we can continue with the cross-examination. So we reconvene in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the turn of the Defence. Who is going to start off?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence of Mr. Pusic has no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. We have no questions for this witness, and we want to thank him for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: The Stojic Defence has no questions for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Praljak Defence as well. We don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We do have some, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could the witness please have the sketch plan in front of him on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, while that's happening, I represent with Ms. Alaburic Mr. Petkovic. Like the Judges, we are simply interested in getting some of the facts clear surrounding these terrible events. Now, first of all, could you indicate, please, on that sketch map exactly where you were standing in the morning when you felt, you said, a bullet pass very close to you. Perhaps you could mark it just with a letter H would be good, I think. I don't think we've used letter H.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said this afternoon that you didn't know where that shot, where that bullet was coming from. And that's right, isn't it? You could not tell where it was coming from.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Sir, the shot was with a silencer. It was muffled. And when it explodes, you don't know where it was, but I didn't think about this, where they were shooting from, until when my daughters were killed and when this hit the bathroom before. I didn't actually think they were shooting at me. It might have been by chance. But -- so you can't say it came from precisely one point. But the shot was in the air, and there was no other way it could have happened and it could have come from, because my daughters were killed. So that's what I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can probably deal with this fairly quickly, I think. The position is this, isn't it, that you have -- as far as you are concerned, you have worked out, after your daughters were shot and from the other information which you got about soldiers, you have worked out where you think it was coming from, but at the time you couldn't have told just from the shot? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: At the time of the shot, especially in the morning. Now, there were a number of shots at one time, because if my three daughters were killed in the same spot or hit in the same spot then there were these three shots, but it was muffled. And that was the direction. There couldn't have been any other direction since they were hit there. And it was day time. It was an open space. That's the only place that you could have had this point and this direction. And I saw the soldiers there when they went in, when they came in the morning. There wasn't any movement during the day below my house or on the opposite side. There was no movement. It was just -- that was the only possible direction that I told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're not saying that you could pinpoint where -- in the morning. We're talking about the morning now. You're not saying you could pinpoint where the shot was coming from, from the sound of the shot that fired the bullet? You're not saying that, are you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Not then, but when this happened, when I heard that it was below the house where I -- where it went past me that the -- and that the shots, the bullets hit the bathroom and the pillar next to this bathroom, and then when my children were killed, then I realised that that was probably the moment when they might have hit me, too. They wanted to hit me too, because it was just a few centimetres away from my ear. But I didn't think about that at the time. I didn't think that anybody shot at me precisely. But later on, I did gain the impression, and I realised that that's what it must have been, that they were shooting at me. But, thank goodness, well, I escaped.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the bullet in the bathroom, that was in somebody else's house a hundred metres away at a different time?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Would you on the sketch plan, please, just draw very simply, you don't need to draw much of it, but just draw very simply the canal as it goes under the road. The canal by which your daughters were shot.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: That is the canal, this passage. You have the asphalt road on top, and then underneath that the canal. So you go -- it's a meter or two underneath the road. There's a canal or a little sort of bridge, underpass. And the canal was by the road. But they were on the road, the asphalt road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. I think we can -- thank you. I think we can describe that, adequately for the transcript, is more or less at right angles going under the road where your daughters were shot. That, I think, is sufficiently descriptive. Now, could you just then indicate -- and perhaps you might do a simple drawing of trees or something like that. You have said in a statement that the persons who killed your daughters were not able to see them immediately when they got on the road because of fruit trees and a huge oak tree. Could you just indicate with a pen on the sketch plan where the fruit trees and the oak tree were that obscured the view.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: From my house to this road here, the road they took is 50 to 60 metres, up to the road. Then they took the road. They were walking along the road for another 50 metres below my property, below the field and the orchard. And when they left the orchard, they took the main road. They walked along the main road. And it's slightly sheltered. There's a vineyard in front, too, and there's an oak tree over the canal, a large oak tree. It was a very big oak tree.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. What I'm going to ask you to do, Mr. Hasic, it can just be a circle as best you can to represent the size and scale of the oak tree. I'd just like you to draw a circle where the oak tree was, and as near to the right size as everything else that you can manage.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it was on the other side of the road, was it, from your house? I'm not -- just draw a circle, please, Mr. Hasic. It's -- a simple circle would be the best of all.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: It's a rather large oak tree, a big one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, I --

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Below the road is the canal and the oak leans over the road. And in front of the -- my orchard and from the oak tree there's 50 or 60 metres where they were. But this is a more open space and there are two houses over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. That's --

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: And you can see this area from the road, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Hasic --

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: -- it's an open other area. You can see from these houses right over that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's stick to my questions. I'm going to ask you, I hope, very short, I hope succinct questions, precise questions, and if you could answer the precise questions. Could you now mark, please, on the sketch plan where those fruit trees were that you also said in your statement obscured the view of the persons who killed your daughters. Just mark them, please. Again, as much to scale as you can.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: That's the orchard, on the left-hand side in front of my house, towards the end of my property, along the roadside, and it was -- they were peaches, peach trees. And above that there was a vineyard. The vineyard was up above. But anyway, these were peach trees along the road. And you could see --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic --

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: You could see them as they emerged --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to invite you to stick with my questions. How high were the peach trees?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: The peach trees were up to three metres high, three and a half, depending. Of course, you picked the fruit from the ground. You can pick the fruit standing on the ground, and then it rises up two and a half, three metres, the tree itself. And they're spaced out three to four metres apart. So one tree next to another along the roadside.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Hasic, can we be clear then? First of all, could you explain how the oak tree ever obscured anybody's view? You're talking about the people who killed your daughter, and you say that the oak tree obscured their view. How did that ever obscure their view since we can see it on the other side of the road? Do you see what my question is? Please explain how the oak tree was ever in the way of the sight line of the people that you say killed your daughter.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I were to take you there, then you could see it and you would see that it is possible. My house is 50 metres away from there, but it's below a hill and so are the others opposite. They are at least 10 metres up above the level of the oak tree. So the oak tree and the orchard, the fruit trees, blocked the view. And I was watching where they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, let's me stop you. The thing is, you're quite right. You know this location. I have never seen it, and I don't know how many other people in court have ever seen it, which is why I'm inviting you to draw as clearly as you can for everybody here on the sketch plan, because that's really all we have to work with. Please explain, then -- it seems -- let me put it to you bluntly. It seems from what you've said as if the fruit trees, if they cut off the sight line of people firing from where you've marked D, would have cut off the sight line more when the girls got to the place where they were shot. Do you see the point I'm putting to you? And implicit in my question is, can you explain what appears to be a real difficulty about your account so far.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: I can say that because when they came out of the orchard, sometimes visibly, other times not visibly, and they might have been 200 metres away because my house is 250 metres away, and the target is more open. The area is more open because you come to the houses where there are no fruit trees. So there's greater visibility because it rises up, the slope, and probably they were more certain of their target there. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you saying that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Stewart, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you saying that in the direction in which the girls were going, the road rises? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Where they -- the area they reach, it was more visible, and 10 metres ahead there's an incline. And there were fig trees opposite these houses, but it was a more open space, more visible. There were these fig trees on the right and the oak down there and the peaches over there. So I would say that it was a more visible spot, although they noticed them 50 metres ahead, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we be clear, Mr. Hasic? You would have had no way of telling from the sound of any shots where the bullets came from that killed your daughters? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, on the basis of the sound in the area you could. It could have come from here or there. But on the basis of the hit and the general direction, it couldn't have been from any other direction. I don't doubt that. And as it was in the air with a muffling, with a muffle, a silencer, perhaps they would have been shooting from another direction but they wouldn't have hit them there, or they wouldn't have hit them where they were hit, in the back of the head, for example. They would have been hit in the chest if they were shooting from another direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There seems to be agreement in that answer Mr. Hasic you could not tell from the sound. On its own, you could not tell from the sound where the bullets came from, could you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of sounds it was sounds in the air with a silencer. You just heard a sound. You couldn't know the direction. But if you look at the target and what was hit, then I know that it came from the direction of where the soldiers came and where they were armed. There was no other way and no other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we be clear about one other thing then, please, Mr. Hasic? You could not yourself tell at any time, could you, from the wounds to your daughters the distance from which the shots came?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, the distance is -- it's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, please answer my question, Mr. Hasic. You could not tell from everything you inspected yourself, it was a horrible experience for you of course, but in looking at your daughters and seeing their wounds, there was no way you could tell the distance from which those shots had been fired, was there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: The distance as is I saw it and from they were, these soldiers, from where their shelter was, 3 to 400 metres, because 120 -- if you look at the electricity poles they are at intervals of 50 metres, which makes it 100, 110 metres from the road and then from the road up to up there, the Stolac-Capljina main road, so it's 10 metres from this main house and from my road, which makes it another 80, so about 300 give or take 350 [as interpreted] metres thereabouts. I didn't measure it, but that would make it from the target to the other, and I saw no other target, nor could there have been any other target.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Any further questions on this topic would be thinly disguised comment so I'll move on to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, which is this: Do you know on the 15th of July there was an attack by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the military placement which is seen on your sketch with the letter C? So that's the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you said on the 15th of July, did you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. My slip. There was a report dated the 15th which is where my wrong date comes from. On the 15th of July in the morning, early in the morning before the time that you experienced being shot at, there was an attack on the headquarters, as you have described it, at letter C marked on the sketch plan. Do you know about that? Do you remember about that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: The C. That's the barracks in Domanovici or the pre-war hospital, the mental hospital, and that's where the army was, the HVO soldiers, and I would see a tank there during those days. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the -- it was the -- it was the headquarters of the, I'll risk it, Knez Domagoj Brigade. I hope that's sufficiently clear. It was their headquarters, wasn't it, at the time? You must know that, Mr. Hasic.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, I know there was a command after the Serbs had left. It was Andrunove houses, two or three metres from the barracks, but I didn't know about this place. Perhaps there was at the time but I wane wear of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We can look at the transcript for when you marked the letter C, Mr. Hasic. Do you know, then, that that morning in an attack 18 HVO soldiers were killed and 25 were wounded? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: I personally don't know that. I know that around Gubavica and the -- there are some commemorative plaques placed there because of the killed Croats. I don't know how many Croats or Muslims there were, 15 or more. I know about my daughters, and I know that on that day and on the following day there were 12 Bosniaks from Bivolje hill who were killed, torched. I've heard about this. I didn't see that myself, but I know where they're buried. I know that they were found there. Twelve of them were found. I can't be precise, I didn't count them, but I these are people I knew, elderly people, and there were young people, too, people of my age group, and there were elderly people, too. That's what I heard at the time. But I also heard there were Croats that were killed since there are these commemorative plaques or monuments raised to them, but I personally don't know how many of them there were. I can't say that there weren't these people who were killed and wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Gubavica, how far is Gubavica from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It should be about 10 kilometres. There's Pijesci in between and then Gubavica. About 10 kilometres. Yes, 8 or 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel said that at the place that you marked with a C there was allegedly an attack in which Croatian soldiers were allegedly killed on the very same day, on the 13th of July. Were you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't aware of that on that day, nor did anyone tell me about that. But this was when I was in a state of shock, and I was very sad. But no one told me about that. I didn't know anything about that. I know nothing about that to this very day. But that people were killed, yes, that's certain. You can see that because of the monuments raised to these people by the road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the question that should have been put to you, but I'll now put it to you, is as follows: As far as you know did the ABiH have any troops in the surroundings of your village? Did the ABiH have any troops there? Were there any armija soldiers who were around your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can tell you that at that time there were no troops. Blagaj and Mostar were 23 or 25 kilometres away. Bobun [phoen] is about 15 kilometres away. There was certainly nothing there that was under the HVO control, and that was also the case for Gubavica. They were there before, but I don't know for sure. They had perhaps someone in Pijesci, about five kilometres from where I was, and then on Gubavica. They were present before that time. But during that period I heard that an attack was launched from Mostar and from Blagaj, but 20 kilometres away -- at a distance of 20 kilometres, no, they weren't present as far as I know. Others could perhaps answer that question, but at that time in July, no, they certainly weren't there. And people had been arrested before July when the armija was there, and then after they had left there were people I knew who came and mentioned people who had had been arrested who were still working. That was in May, a month or two earlier, and clashes had already broken out in my village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in your village would it have been possible for a villager to be armed? Could any of the villagers have been armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at that time I myself don't know. No one was under the age of 50. Well, it doesn't matter. A 50-year-old can also be a soldier, or a 60-year-old, but as for soldiers, people with weapons, no, they were already in the camp, or if not, they had fled. They were in Blagaj or Mostar. That's what I know. But when these clashes broke out, and this is what we heard, naturally Blagaj or Mostar, well, an attack was launched on Gubavica and then Bivolje hill. Those were the clashes at the time. But I wasn't aware of them being present here or I didn't see them. I'm certain they weren't present in my hamlet at least. As for other places, well, on the whole the army was present in Blagaj and Mostar. There were perhaps commands there and so on. But amongst us there were about 20, 25 families. I don't think there were any soldiers. There were Croats with us. They would have known. We went from house to house. We would have seen them if they had been there I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, you've told us already it comes to this doesn't it between the 1st and the 13th of July, you were strongly concerned to keep a low profile, stay out of the way, avoid being arrested yourself, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When I heard about people going to the market, well, it was July, we didn't have grapes but we had peaches that were rotting. I had tons that were rotting. I can't be precise, but on that day I had left these goods in a garage in the car and I couldn't go to the market. Then my women -- my wife came and said, I should transport the peaches, but I didn't. And I didn't dare to do that as of the 1st of July, because I had heard about people being arrested, vehicles being seized, goods being kept in Capljina. And as of that point in time, naturally I tried not to go to certain places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, although you've told us that you did not know yourself at the time, please confirm, it appears that you do now accept from what you have subsequently heard and learnt that there was in fact an attack early on the 13th of July on the installation which is in the vicinity of letter C at the top left-hand corner of your sketch. That's right, isn't it? You have heard and you do know that there was.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: I know about that attack from the barracks in the direction of Capljina, below the cemetery. It's about a kilometre from Domanovici. I have some property down there, but on that occasion I didn't go there. But I heard that mines had been laid on the road and that the army had -- the armija had done this. I wasn't there then and I didn't see that, but I know where it is. Later, I saw that area when it had been repaired, but on that day, on the 13th and 14th, well, I don't remember mines having been laid then, because I passed through to Capljina with my colleague. As I have said, I went to fetch the coffins, and the road was practicable. And it was in Domanovici. There was a cemetery about a kilometre away. That's what they said, though. That's what I heard but on the 14th at about 9.00 or 10.00, we set off. Well, it was around 9.00. We set off in the direction of Capljina, and that was on the 14th, and we passed through without any problems. But I do know where this location is, but we left that morning, on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So let's try and summarise. Do you agree that on the 13th of July and through to the 15th of July there was in fact quite significant fighting going on in or very close to where you lived, by which I mean within a kilometre?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: I left on the 14th, so I didn't hear anything else. But I believe there was some sort of fighting or -- no, in fact I didn't hear about fighting on the 13th or 14th. I was in the camp by the 14th. Anything is possible, but no one told me that these 12 men were killed between the 12th and the 13th and thrown into a pit and burnt, that tyres had been thrown in on top of them. That was found out later. But there were these 12 people killed, these Croats. But was it on the 14th or the 15th, well, then anything is possible. I was in the camp. I can't say that there was no fighting on the 15th, but my wife didn't tell me anything about people being killed there or about fighting, at least not in my area. As Gubavica and further up there, well, I can't say that that was not the case or that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How far is Bivolje Brdo from your house?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: Well, it consists of two parts. It's about three kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question. How far from your house is Bivolje Brdo?

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: The nearest point -- there's part of the hill that's not visible, but the close of the house at the time -- well, there is one those closer now because there's a new Croatian settlement. But the closest one is about 200 metres from my fence, perhaps, but under a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Give us a distance. In 1993, I mean. I'm sorry, I should have made that clearer.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: The closest point would have been a kilometre, or we could say over a kilometre, over 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your -- this may be my last question but no guarantees. In your statement, and for anybody looking at it it's in the middle of page 3 of the English version, you said, "I can also guarantee that there were no army of Bosnia and Herzegovina soldiers in our village." The strictly correct position is this, isn't it, that you can't guarantee. The most you can say is you didn't actually see any with your own eyes; is that right? That's the most you can claim.

utterances.speaker: HASAN HASIC
utterances.text: I personally didn't see any soldiers in that area of mine, in that part of the hamlet. I didn't see any members of the armija apart from the people I saw in the morning in those neighbouring houses, the Croatian houses across the road at a distance about 200 or 250 metres from my house. I saw those soldiers in the morning, 6.00, 7.00, or 8.00, it doesn't really matter. And later I didn't see any soldiers who were of the armija or in that part, at least, of my village or in those houses that I went to in the area where my daughters were killed. But further away, well, as I have said, there were these two Croats whom they brought there, and they said that there were these armija soldiers from another place who had come but they left. They were apparently imprisoned, but they were in Meso Hasic house they would sit down with him and then return to a village a little further from Bivolje Brdo or Bivolje hill, perhaps. I spoke to them. I knew them. But I didn't see any other soldiers apart from the soldiers I saw in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Hasic, please, when you went to Capljina on the 14th of July, were you stopped anywhere on the road? Were there any road checks or roadblocks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said, Rafo Popovic, a Croat and I set off in his lorry. I also had my lorry, but I didn't go alone. He was with me. We didn't have any problems to reach Capljina. It was just when we were in Domanovici. That was on the following day, on the 14th. There were 50 or a hundred men in uniform. They were armed. They were soldiers. They didn't have any vehicles. They were waiting there by the crossroads where we set off for Capljina. That's where they were positioned. And then later, I suppose that's when these people -- these 12 people were killed, and then there were these clashes that the gentleman has mentioned. Perhaps that is what happened. But I didn't have any problems to get to Capljina. I stayed in Capljina then, and I can't say anything else as a result. There were no check-points, though, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just to make sure, these some 50 soldiers gathered at the crossroad, were they HVO or ABiH, armija, or HVO, or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] HVO soldiers. I know their names. They are familiar people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome. Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you knew their names because among the 50 HVO soldiers there were villagers whom you knew. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There was the son of this person whose father had been taken to Meho's. His son was at the crossroads, and then there were others. Merdzan, I know him - his mother was from my village; then there was this sister of Popovic's - he approached me. He kissed me and cried, just as I would do. There were two Buntics who arrived in arrived in a vehicle. They were in a car. There were these neighbours from where my daughters were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: There is something which looks strange in the transcript. One reads, "There was this sister of Popovic," and it goes on, "He approached me. He kissed me." Maybe it's a translation problem, but sisters normally are she. Was it a sister's husband or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Rafo Popovic's sister, the mother of the son whose name was Marko Merdzan. The mother of Merdzan is Popovic's sister, and her son embraced me there and expressed his sympathy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Hvala ljepo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomasegovic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the Prosecution have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: No re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this completes your testimony. On before of my colleagues, and I myself, I would like to thank you for your assistance, especially in light of the difficult experiences you have had. You have our deepest sympathy for the fate of your family members. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm also sorry that that happened and that perhaps innocent people are victims or were taken to be more responsible than those who were actually responsible. These are inhuman acts, what I experienced. Well, even after all of these experiences, it's difficult. There are other people. As to what they did, it's inhuman. It hasn't been proven. There are many who are highly educated. Perhaps they were educated, act inappropriately, how should I put it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, could you escort the witness out the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish you all the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, according to the weather report the sun will be shining in Sarajevo tomorrow. The day after tomorrow it will be cloudy, and on Friday it will snow. Given that the sun will be shining tomorrow, will it be possible for the plane to take off? And I should point out that in fact it was foggy today and it was 1 degree Celsius in the morning and 15 degrees in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well -- thank you for that, Mr. President. At this point we're actually now hoping that the weather is similarly clear in Zagreb because the witnesses are on their way to Zagreb to be flown from that airport. I can again report at this point that we clearly have two witnesses scheduled for tomorrow. The witnesses that are travelling tomorrow should be available to testify on Thursday. We don't have at this point any witnesses on Wednesday. I anticipate that the witness that's currently scheduled for Thursday will be testifying on Monday of next week, and we will take -- I'll have a meeting with my team tomorrow morning and make some decisions about how we're going to squeeze an extra witness into next week. Most likely we will make a decision that one or more of the witnesses scheduled for next week might be a 92 ter witness rather than a viva voce witness, but I should have some additional information for the Trial Chamber and the parties tomorrow when we meet. But again, the two witnesses for tomorrow as scheduled will be testifying. There will be no witnesses available on Wednesday. We will then have the Wednesday witnesses on Thursday and the Thursday witness on Monday of next week, assuming that the weather in Zagreb holds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Any other issues to raise as we still have some time left? Mr. Mundis, any other issues? Defence counsel? Very well. In that case, we will resume our work tomorrow at the hearing that starts at 2.15 p.m.
